title: A Computer
You Can Draw
slides.dek: Wireworld is a cellular automaton with four cell states and one rule for moving a spark down a wire. That is the whole machine. Out of it fall a clock that beats forever, a valve that passes only one way, and a logic gate that really computes, and once you have a gate you can build a computer out of nothing but wire.

slides.body: Wireworld has four cell states. A cell is *empty*, or a *conductor* (wire waiting to be used), or an *electron head* (the bright edge of a spark), or an *electron tail* (the part already fading back to wire). One rule runs on every cell at once: empty stays empty; a head becomes a tail; a tail becomes a conductor, so a spark is always two cells long and can never sit still; and a conductor lights into a head only if *exactly one or two* of its eight neighbours are heads. That last clause is the whole trick. It is why a spark runs cleanly down a wire instead of smearing out, and, later, why a gate can tell one pulse from two.

Bend a wire into a *ring* and drop in one spark and you have a clock: it cannot stop, so it loops forever and taps out one pulse per lap. Seven cells in the right knot make a *diode*, a pulse passes one way and is swallowed the other, pure consequence of shape. A *T* copies one pulse into two. But the payoff is *exclusive-or*. Send a pulse into one input and it threads the crossing and reaches the output: one. Send a pulse into *both* inputs on the same tick and the two heads over-fill the central cells, all decay to tails together, and none survives to cross: zero. Signals that agree cancel; signals that differ get through. That is why a real Wireworld machine clocks every wire in lockstep.

lines.sub: rotate format back to app after #040. reopen the emergence-into-computation vein and show what #023 game-of-life claimed but could not: cells that visibly compute. wireworld (silverman, 1987) is a four-state automaton built to carry a current

one stepWW(g,W,H) engine, four states, the 1-or-2-heads clause. a 46x30 paint board (wire / spark / erase brushes) preloaded with six machine-found circuits: a ring clock, a 7-cell diode, a fan-out, an OR merge, and a live XOR gate

checked offline first: a pulse advances exactly one cell per tick; the ring clock traps one electron forever; a brute-force search found a clean one-way diode and an XOR gate whose truth table is exactly 0,1,1,0, the 1-xor-1 case a genuine head-on collision

four states, one rule,
and a gate that
*really computes.*
slides.sub: Paint on a 46 by 30 board and watch one rule run. Load the clock (a ring trapping one electron forever), the diode (one-way by shape alone), the fan-out and the OR merge, then poke the XOR gate, pulse A, pulse B, pulse both, and see equal inputs cancel while different ones cross. Every circuit was found by brute-force search and re-simulated in your browser on load, nothing stored, nothing fetched. The end of this road is a full computer, built in Wireworld by Owen and Moore, that prints the primes.
